Q3 2026 EARNINGS CONFERENCE CALL




                                   Q3 2026 EARNINGS
                                   CONFERENCE CALL
                                   November 3, 2026
 FORWARD LOOKING INFORMATION
Fortis includes forward-looking information in this presentation within the meaning of applicable Canadian securities laws and forward-looking
statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 (collectively referred to as "forward-looking information").
Forward-looking information reflects expectations of Fortis management regarding future growth, results of operations, performan ce and business
prospects and opportunities. Wherever possible, words such as anticipates, believes, budgets, could, estimates, expects, fore casts, intends, may,
might, plans, projects, schedule, should, target, will, would, and the negative of these terms, and other similar terminology or expressions have been
used to identify the forward-looking information, which includes, without limitation: forecast Capital Expenditures for 2026 and 2027-2031; expected
timing, outcome, and impact of legal and regulatory proceedings; forecast five-year CAGR to 2031; annual dividend growth guidance through 2031;
forecast Rate Base for 2026 through 2031; forecast three-year CAGR to 2029; the expectation that the proportion of ITC's FERC-regulated assets in the
Corporation's consolidated Rate Base will increase during the Capital Plan period; expected nature, timing, benefits, and cos ts of certain opportunities
above and beyond the Capital Plan at ITC, including investments associated with the MISO LRTP Tranche 2.1 projects, other MISO LRTP and MTEP
projects, and customer connections associated with load growth; expected in-service dates and total cost of the MARS project; expected nature,
timing, benefits, and costs of certain opportunities above and beyond the Capital Plan at UNS Energy, including investments a ssociated with load
growth for new and existing customers, integrated resource plans, and FERC-regulated transmission; expected timing and resources for TEP to serve
load pursuant to an energy supply agreement with its data center customer; estimated costs of incremental generation and asso ciated transmission
investments associated with the approximately 550 MW high-load-factor customer scenario in TEP's IRP; planned resource additions under TEP's and
UNS Electric's base case IRPs; projected average system cost per kWh under various scenarios included in TEP's IRP; TEP's planned retirement of coal-
fired generation by 2032; TEP's aspirational goal of net-zero direct greenhouse gas emissions by 2050; expected timing of the ACC acknowledgement
of IRPs in 2027; expected nature, timing, benefits, and costs of certain opportunities above and beyond the Capital Plan at F ortisBC, including
investments associated with the Tilbury LNG Expansion post-2031, Regional Transmission Pipeline Expansion, and customer and load growth in the
Okanagan electric service territory; estimated potential incremental capital above and beyond the Capital Plan; expected and potential impacts on
rates associated with various affordability initiatives, including O&M savings targets at Central Hudson, beneficial load gro wth at ITC Midwest and TEP,
capital optimization related to the UNS Springerville Natural Gas Generation, and rate benefits associated with LNG projects at FortisBC and the Eagle
Mountain Pipeline Project; expected sources of funding for the Capital Plan, including common equity provided through the DRIP at current
participation levels; the expectation of a consistent capital structure over the planning period; the expectation that the fu nding plan supports existing
investment-grade credit ratings; planned re-establishment of the short-form base shelf prospectus and ATM Program in early 2027; forecast credit
metrics for 2026 and 2027-2031; forecast Capital Expenditures for 2027-2031 by business unit; forecast capital expenditures for pre-2027, 2027-2031,
post-2031, total project cost and estimated completion dates of Major Capital Projects, including ITC MISO LRTP – Tranche 1, ITC MISO LRTP – Tranche
2.1, ITC Big Cedar Load Expansion, UNS Transmission Project at TEP, UNS Gas Generation Project at UNS Electric, UNS Springerville Natural Gas
Generation, FortisBC Tilbury 1B Project, FortisBC LNG Storage Tank Expansion, FortisBC AMI Project, and FortisBC Eagle Mountain Pipeline Project;
expected construction timing of Tilbury 1B; expected stakeholder consultation related to Tilbury Phase 2 LNG Expansion; potential additional capacity
of, ability to supply domestic or bulk LNG export markets from, and expected staged development of the Tilbury Phase 2 Liquef action Expansion;
forecast Rate Base for 2026 through 2031 and five-year CAGR to 2031 by business unit; estimated impact of the U.S. dollar-to-Canadian dollar
exchange rate, inclusive of hedging activities, on the Capital Plan and EPS; the Corporation's commitment to a coal-free generation mix by 2032; the
Corporation's 2050 net-zero greenhouse gas emissions target; forecast debt maturities for 2027-2036; the expectation of a declining dividend payout
ratio over time; the expected strategic focus of the Corporation on organic growth; the expected regulatory framework for For tisAlberta following the
current PBR term; expected nature, timing, benefits, and costs of certain opportunities at FortisAlberta, including investmen ts associated with load
growth, large load interconnections, reliability and wildfire mitigation; the intention to maintain a buffer above rating age ncy credit metric thresholds;
the potential use of the ATM Program, hybrid capital, and other financing alternatives to fund capital above and beyond the C apital Plan, and the
expected timing of any such funding requirements; estimated capacity to issue additional hybrid capital; the expected impact of the proposed federal
productivity deduction on the Corporation's credit metrics and on customer rates at its Canadian utilities; and the expected timing of a final
investment decision and permitting associated with the Tilbury Phase 2 Liquefaction Expansion.

 Forward-looking information involves significant risks, uncertainties, and assumptions. Certain material factors or assumptions have been applied in
drawing the conclusions contained in the forward-looking information including, without limitation: the successful execution of the Capital Plan; no
material capital project or financing cost overrun; sufficient human resources to deliver service and execute the Capital Plan; the realization of
additional opportunities beyond the Capital Plan; no significant variability in interest rates; no material changes in the as sumed U.S. dollar-to-Canadian
dollar exchange rate; the Board exercising its discretion to declare dividends, taking into account the financial performance and condition of the
Corporation; reasonable legal and regulatory decisions and the expectation of regulatory stability; no significant operationa l disruptions or
environmental liability or upset; the continued ability to maintain the performance of the electricity and gas systems; no se vere and prolonged
economic downturn; sufficient liquidity and capital resources; the ability to hedge exposures to fluctuations in foreign exch ange rates, natural gas
prices and electricity prices; the continued availability of natural gas, fuel, coal and electricity supply; continuation of power supply and capacity
purchase contracts; no significant changes in government energy policies, environmental laws and regulations that could have a material negative
impact; maintenance of adequate insurance coverage; the ability to obtain and maintain licenses and permits; retention of exi sting service areas; no
significant changes in tax laws and the continued tax deferred treatment of earnings from the Corporation's foreign operation s; continued
maintenance of information technology infrastructure and no material breach of cybersecurity; continued favourable relations with Indigenous
Peoples; and favourable labour relations.

 Fortis cautions readers that a number of factors could cause actual results, performance or achievements to differ materially from the results
discussed or implied in the forward-looking information. These factors should be considered carefully, and undue reliance should not be placed on the
forward-looking information. For additional information with respect to certain of these risks or factors, reference should be made to the continuous
disclosure materials filed from time to time by the Corporation with Canadian securities regulatory authorities and the Secur ities and Exchange
Commission. All forward-looking information herein is given as of the date of this presentation. Fortis disclaims any intention or obligation to update
or revise any forward-looking information, whether as a result of new information, future events or otherwise.

Unless otherwise specified, all financial information is in Canadian dollars and rate base refers to midyear rate base.

Note: U.S. dollar-denominated five-year Capital Plan and forecast rate base converted at a forecast USD:CAD foreign exchange rate of 1.35 for
2027-2031.

 FORTIS INC. FQ3 2026 EARNINGS CALL NOV 03, 2026




Presentation
Operator
Thank you for standing by. This is Betsy, the conference operator. Welcome to the Fortis Inc. Third Quarter 2026 Results and New
Five-year Capital Outlook Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] The conference is being recorded. [Operator Instructions]

I would now like to turn the conference over to Stephanie Amaimo, Vice President, Investor Relations. Please go ahead, Ms. Amaimo.
Stephanie A. Amaimo
Vice President of Investor Relations
Thanks, Betsy, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Fortis' Third Quarter 2026 Results and New Five-year Capital Outlook
Conference Call. I'm joined by David Hutchens, President and CEO; Jocelyn Perry, Executive VP and CFO; other members of the
senior management team as well as CEOs from certain subsidiaries.

Before we begin today's call, I want to remind everyone that the discussion will include forward-looking information, which is subject
to the cautionary statement contained in the supporting slide show. Actual results can differ materially from the forecast projections
included in the forward-looking information presented today.

Non-GAAP financial measures referenced in our prepared remarks are reconciled to the related U.S. GAAP financial measures in our
third quarter 2026 MD&A.

Also, unless otherwise specified, all financial information referenced is in Canadian dollars.

With that, I will turn the call over to David.
David Gerard Hutchens
President, CEO & Director
Thank you, and good morning, everyone. This past quarter has been one of the busiest and most positive I can remember during my
tenure as CEO, leading to meaningful progress and significant opportunities for our business going forward. We're also happy to put
another strong quarter behind us.

Operationally, we continue to provide safe and reliable service to our customers and invested $4.2 billion in our systems year-to-date.
For the full year, we expect to invest approximately $6 billion, up $400 million from our plan. And we delivered earnings per share for
the third quarter of $0.92.

And today, we are unveiling our new 5-year capital plan, our largest to date. Big news hit in the quarter with respect to our Tilbury site
in British Columbia and ITC being awarded a competitive bid project in Iowa. And today, we announced that our Board of Directors
declared a fourth quarter dividend increase of 4%, marking 53 years of dividend increases.

Before getting into the details of our new 5-year outlook, I will turn the call over to Jocelyn to speak to our third quarter results.
Jocelyn H. Perry
Executive VP & CFO
Thank you, David, and good morning, everyone. For the quarter, reported earnings were $474 million or $0.92 per common share.
And on a year-to-date basis, reported earnings were $1.4 billion or $2.69 per common share. As you can see on the slide, reported
earnings in 2025 included income taxes and closing costs of $0.06 per share associated with the disposition of FortisTCI. Excluding
this impact, adjusted EPS for the quarter was up $0.05 and year-to-date adjusted EPS was up $0.06.

On the next slide, you will see the adjusted EPS drivers for the quarter by segment. At ITC, EPS increased by $0.03, driven by rate
base growth and lower stock-based compensation expense, partially offset by higher finance costs. Our U.S. Electric and Gas segment
contributed a $0.02 increase, mainly driven by UNS Energy. The growth in Arizona was due to higher electricity sales associated with
residential and industrial usage and customer growth.

The timing of operating costs and lower income taxes associated with the amortization of investment tax credits on the battery storage
project also contributed to the increase. Moderating this was the impact of milder weather quarter-over-quarter and regulatory lag
associated with rate base growth not yet reflected in rates.

At Central Hudson, earnings were largely consistent quarter-over-quarter as rate base growth, the timing of costs and a contribution
to a customer benefit fund in 2025 were offset by a favorable regulatory adjustment made in the third quarter of 2025 upon
implementation of the most recent rate order.

Our Western Canadian utilities increased EPS by $0.02 in the quarter, driven by rate base growth as well as lower income tax expense
at FortisAlberta.

And for our Other Electric segment, EPS decreased by $0.01, largely due to the disposition of FortisTCI in September 2025.

The Corporate and Other segment reflect net unrealized losses on derivative contracts compared to unrealized gains in 2025, the
timing of income tax recoveries and the disposition of Fortis Belize in the fourth quarter of 2025.

Foreign Exchange had a $0.01 favorable impact for the quarter, and higher weighted average shares issued under the dividend
reinvestment plan and ATM program impacted EPS by $0.01.

And as noted on the slide, the 2025 disposition of our assets in Turks and Caicos and Belize lowered EPS by $0.02 in the quarter, net
of finance cost savings.

Year-to-date results were mainly driven by the same factors discussed for the quarter with a few additional items to note. For the 9-
month period, Central Hudson was up $0.04, primarily due to rate base growth and the timing of costs, partially offset by the favorable
regulatory adjustment in 2025 as discussed earlier.

At UNS, EPS was down $0.01, which reflects lower margin on wholesale sales and higher operating costs in addition to the other
items noted for the quarter.

And lastly, the impact of Foreign Exchange was $0.03 and the impact of the 2025 dispositions net of finance cost savings was $0.05
year-to-date.

Turning next to our regulatory update. In October, the ACC administrative law judge issued a recommended opinion and order in
TEP's general rate application, recommending an allowed ROE of 9.65% and a 55% common equity component of capital structure.
We currently have an allowed ROE of 9.55% and a 54% equity component of capital structure. The order also recommended an
annual formulaic rate adjustment mechanism with a range of plus or minus 50 basis points around the allowed ROE, the inclusion of
post-test year adjustments, the elimination of certain adjustor mechanisms and the deferral of certain costs associated with Roadrunner
Reserve II for future recovery. The ALJ's recommendation proposes implementation of new rates by December 1 and is subject to
ACC approval, which is anticipated later this month.

I'll now turn the call back to David to cover key elements of our new 5-year capital plan.
David Gerard Hutchens
President, CEO & Director
Thank you, Jocelyn. Our new $32.2 billion 5-year capital plan is $3.4 billion higher than our previous plan. Our 5-year rate base
CAGR is 7.5%, up 50 basis points compared to the prior plan. We have also extended our annual dividend growth guidance of
4% to 6% through 2031. This new plan builds on the growth momentum across our high-quality footprint while keeping customer
affordability top of mind.

The growth in our 5-year plan is largely driven by transmission and LNG investments. At ITC, the $1.7 billion increase was primarily
driven by projects associated with MISO's Tranche 2.1 long-range transmission plan, along with higher baseline reliability projects
and new interconnections.

At FortisBC, the $1 billion increase primarily reflects investments in LNG infrastructure, including the Tilbury Phase 1B liquefaction
expansion and the new Tilbury LNG Storage Tank.

The remaining increase is driven by customer growth and reliability investments across our footprint.

The new plan is highly executable with approximately 75% directed towards transmission and distribution investments and critical
infrastructure that supports stable and predictable returns. The capital program is low risk and comprised of 100% regulated projects
and includes 11 major capital projects.

Consolidated rate base is expected to increase from $45 billion in 2026 to approximately $56 billion in 2029 and $64 billion in 2031,
yielding 3- and 5-year compound average growth rates of 7.7% and 7.5%, respectively.

Last month, we were pleased to see MISO award ITC the Tranche 2.1 competitive bid project in Iowa, known as the MARS project.
This allows ITC to design, build, own and operate the project, which includes approximately 300 miles of new 345 and 765 kV
transmission lines in ITC's service territory. The project's total investment is estimated at $1 billion with approximately $500 million
included in our new 5-year capital plan with the balance expected post 2031.
Now, I will take a few minutes to speak in more detail on the capital plans at our 3 largest utilities. ITC's capital plan of $11.6 billion
is the largest in the company's history and supports 5-year rate base growth of 8.6%, up 50 basis points compared to the prior plan.
ITC's regulated assets currently represent about 1/3 of our consolidated rate base with that portion expected to trend upwards over the
plan as ITC continues to deliver our strongest rate base growth.

Significant opportunities above and beyond the base plan exists at ITC, including approximately USD 2.9 billion to USD 3.4 billion
post 2031 for Tranche 2.1 projects assigned through rights of first refusal as well as approximately $500 million for the MARS project
that I mentioned earlier.

ITC may also realize future opportunities associated with projects as part of the ongoing MISO and SPP transmission planning
processes.

Other potential areas of growth include customer connections associated with over 10,000 megawatts of load growth for proposed data
centers, industrial customers and economic development projects in various stages of development across their footprint. This is up
from 8,000 megawatts last quarter.

With significant investments underway and a robust pipeline of future growth opportunities, ITC is well positioned to deliver
sustained long-term growth through this transformative period of transmission expansion.
Turning to UNS Energy. Their capital plan of $5.6 billion supports 5-year rate base growth of 7.4%. Like the prior plan, investments
are spread across the value chain. Notably, over 2/3 of the capital plan is concentrated in transmission and distribution infrastructure
with the balance consisting of generation and other investments.

As for opportunities above and beyond the plan, we continue to see strong interest from both new and existing customers across our
service territory. At TEP, we have one approved energy supply agreement associated with approximately 300 megawatts of data
center load that is expected to begin ramping in 2027 and will be supported by existing and planned resources, including renewable
generation and energy storage already in service or under development.

Beyond this initial agreement and the subsequent phases under negotiations with the customer, our Arizona service territories
are experiencing strong demand associated with mining, industrial development, electrification and broader commercial and
residential growth. These opportunities have the potential to drive additional investments in generation, transmission and distribution
infrastructure over time.

Last week, both TEP and UNS Electric filed their 2026 integrated resource plans with the Arizona Corporation Commission, outlining
their plans to meet customers' projected energy needs over the next 15 years.

TEP's base case scenario prioritizes affordability and assumes average annual sales growth of 5.7% through 2031. It also includes up
to USD 1.3 billion of opportunity above the capital plan through 2031, subject to RFP processes.

Additionally, to evaluate the significant growth potential I previously mentioned, TEP included a high-growth scenario in its
integrated resource plan that would require approximately 800 megawatts of new generation and require up to USD 1.5 billion of
incremental investments. These opportunities are not currently reflected in our base capital plan, but represent meaningful long-term
growth potential for the business. It is important to note that this high-growth scenario is very beneficial to TEP's customers with the
lowest rates of all scenarios as seen on the graph to the right. In terms of the next steps, the stakeholder process will begin next year,
and we expect ACC acknowledgment in the third quarter of 2027.

Turning now to British Columbia, where investments in natural gas and LNG infrastructure are driving strong growth at FortisBC.
FortisBC's $6 billion capital plan includes investments to maintain system reliability and integrity alongside major LNG and advanced
metering infrastructure projects. The capital plan supports rate base growth of 7.9%, up from 6% in the prior plan.

There are a number of projects underway at our Tilbury site with additional opportunities for growth. Back in July, we received an
Order in Council for a larger Phase 1B liquefaction project as well as the Marine Jetty to support LNG marine fueling in the Port of
Vancouver. Total investments for this project are expected to be approximately $1.7 billion.

In September, FortisBC received environmental approvals for its Phase 2 expansion, including investing up to $1.1 billion in the
Tilbury LNG Storage Tank Expansion project. This 3 Bcf storage tank and associated regasification improves resilience and supports
affordability for our customers. Phase 2 also provides an opportunity of up to 2.5 million tonnes per annum of additional liquefaction
capacity to serve emerging domestic and export LNG markets. We have the flexibility to develop this project in stages, and we
estimate an investment opportunity in the range of $2 billion to $4 billion depending on market demand, and the majority of this
expenditure is expected beyond 2031. We continue to work through permitting and our final investment decision.

Development at the Tilbury site has been many years in the making and represents the exceptional work by our team in British
Columbia to expand the use of their gas network to produce regulated LNG that lowers carbon emissions and improves customer
affordability. Bringing it all together, we are focused on executing our new 5-year plan while working to advance our robust growth
pipeline.

I will now turn the call back to Jocelyn.
Jocelyn H. Perry
Executive VP & CFO
As we prepared our new 5-year outlook, customer affordability remains front and center. In addition to efficiently funding our capital
plan, several of our key customer affordability initiatives include O&M savings targets, low-growth projects like in Iowa and Arizona,
least-cost capital projects like the Springerville Repowering Project and the continued delivery of customer conservation programs.
And with increased sales of LNG through the expansion of our Tilbury facility, we expect to continue to provide rate benefits for our
customers. We continue to take a disciplined approach to funding the $3.4 billion increase in the new 5-year plan, together with the
$400 million increase in our 2026 capital plan.
We advanced a portion of our funding requirements in 2026 through the issuance of USD 1 billion of hybrids and approximately $260
million of ATM equity in the third quarter. Over the next 5 years, as you can see on the funding pie chart, our capital plan is expected
to be funded primarily through cash from operations and debt issued at our regulated utilities. Our dividend reinvestment plan remains
the foundation of our equity needs over the 5-year plan. We do expect to issue approximately $250 million of ATM equity over the
next 12 months, subject to market conditions.

Overall, our funding plan is designed to support our strong investment-grade credit ratings. Our credit profile is underpinned by
a diverse, high-quality portfolio of regulated utilities with 95% of our assets in transmission and distribution across constructive
regulatory jurisdictions, providing stable and predictable cash flows. The plan supports average S&P FFO to debt metrics above 12%
over the 5-year period with improving financial flexibility in the latter years, as well as average Fitch FFO leverage of approximately
5.9x. Taken together, our high-quality regulated portfolio, disciplined funding approach and improving credit metrics positions us to
execute the capital plan while maintaining a strong credit profile.

Today, we announced the declaration by our Board of Directors of a fourth quarter dividend of $0.665, representing a 4% increase.
This brings us to 53 consecutive years of increases in dividends paid, a track record that we are very proud of. With our strong
dividend history and regulated growth strategy, we are extending our 4% to 6% annual dividend growth guidance through 2031.

I'll now turn the call back to David to wrap up.
David Gerard Hutchens
President, CEO & Director
When we think about the Fortis investment proposition, it really comes down to sustainable growth supported by our high-quality
portfolio of regulated utilities. We have strong rate base growth, a robust growth pipeline and a transparent funding plan. We're
investing to strengthen the resiliency of our systems and ensure they can reliably and affordably meet customers' evolving energy
needs. We are doing that from a strong foundation: 100% regulated utilities, solid investment-grade credit ratings, regulatory and
geographic diversity and a proven track record, all the right pieces to provide long-term value to our customers and shareholders.

That concludes my remarks. I will now turn the call back over to Stephanie.
Stephanie A. Amaimo
Vice President of Investor Relations
Thank you, David. This concludes the presentation. At this time, we'd like to open the call to address questions from the investment
community.

Question and Answer
Operator
[Operator Instructions] The first question today comes from Maurice Choy with RBC.
Maurice Choy
RBC Capital Markets, Research Division
Recognizing that there's a lot of good growth in ITC as well as FortisBC, I do want to touch on the large load opportunity at UNS
Energy. In the past, you've highlighted a potential of incremental generation costing about $1.5 billion to $2 billion through 2030.
And as I look at the presentation today on Slide 14, I see that there is up to $1.5 billion of investment. So assuming these numbers
are apples-to-apples, is it fair to suggest that your new plan includes some, but still not very much large load-related CapEx? And
maybe as a quick follow-up, if that's true, in the spirit of today's U.S. elections, how do you see your outlook for this remaining growth
CapEx being shaped by the election if it does proceed as the poll suggests?
David Gerard Hutchens
President, CEO & Director
Yes. Thanks, Maurice, and thanks for the question. No, actually, there is no additional capital in our plan related to any data center
growth in Arizona. The difference is just the size that we were assuming. So when we talk about the estimated $1.5 billion of
additional investment opportunities, it was based on adding a certain amount of load to our integrated resource plan. So we were
trying to -- we basically ran a model to try to get numbers based on probably something that was in the middle of that range that we
were looking at before.

So when we talked about -- when we talk about the projects in Arizona, we have the existing 300-megawatt ESA. We have additional
opportunity for investment at that site, which we always put kind of around that 300 megawatts to build that total site out to, say,
500 or 600 megawatts. And then, we were always talking about a second site as well that is still looking at building out there in the
north part of the Tucson area. And that one we estimated at 500 to 700 megawatts. So when we put in that $1.5 billion to $2 billion, it
was more like that whole bucket of projects. And here, we are actually just taking a little bit smaller portion of it for that high-growth
scenario.

And then -- so to opine on the election outcome and whether or not and what that might mean for data center development, I think
as we sit here today and as folks go to the polls in the U.S., obviously, the data center topic has been very front of mind for a lot of
voters and a lot of politicians. What I'm hoping is that we can hopefully find our way away from rhetoric and look at the real positive
benefits that we see from data centers. As long as they're done right, as long as there's no cost shifting, as long as there's net benefit to
our customers and all the environmental and water and the rest of those things are addressed by the communities that they're going in.
But when you have these large loads come in, it makes your system more efficient and saves customers money.

We're seeing that in Iowa, as you saw on the slide, talking about that 20% reduction in those rates there. We see it in Arizona, even
though we're not making any additional investments for the first 300 megawatts of data center that we have there. We're seeing a $13
per month benefit. So all of those things hopefully will flow through and people will see the proof and the positive nature of what
this -- of what some of these large loads can do. And it's not just large data centers, it's large load and high-capacity factor customers
like we're seeing for LNG in British Columbia. So there are some positive benefits, but I think no one wants to talk about them until
tomorrow.
Maurice Choy
RBC Capital Markets, Research Division
Understood. That all makes sense. And maybe I could just finish it off with a question on funding, particularly given the greater
growth that you have in front of you. I know that the DRIP program is still the main tool that you use for your common equity
requirements. And in the past, you said that, you know, all options are on the table if CapEx rises, including asset sales and
considering the options there. How should we think about your use of ATM moving forward? You've initiated that as part of your Q3
period using that vehicle versus discrete issuances. And perhaps more broadly, I see the 12.3% FFO to debt average, but how do you
philosophically size what is the right buffer versus your 12% threshold?
Jocelyn H. Perry
Executive VP & CFO

 FORTIS INC. FQ3 2026 EARNINGS CALL NOV 03, 2026



Thanks, Maurice. Yes. So we do have the ATM program available. And the DRIP, as you said, has been quite healthy and provided
most of the equity needs that we have. Look, we anchor everything back to, I think, the credit metrics that you referred to. And what
is the right buffer? It takes a lot to move the metrics given the size of Fortis. But, yes, we've said that we'd like to have a 50 to 75 basis
point buffer above those metric thresholds. And really, it's not any one thing that I think would happen with Fortis that would kick us
past those buffer limits. It's more about if things change in the world and the thresholds just change at the rating agency level and not
anything to do with Fortis. But we do anchor sort of our funding plan around holding that kind of level of buffer.

So when I think about the ATM going forward, as we listen to David talk about all those, I guess, above and beyond the plan
opportunities in each of our regulated utilities, back to what you said Maurice, we will be looking at everything. ATM will be one
piece of that to fund that, but again, anchored back to our credit profile and our credit metrics. We also have room for hybrid, more
hybrids in our cap structure. We only have about 6% in our cap structure today. And as you know, I mean, there's room to add more
there. And so again, no real secret to how we think about funding. We try to maintain the buffer. But when we start to see and get
visibility on the growth above and beyond the current plan that we'll have, we'll assess what options are in front of us, and we'll choose
it once we can see the new growth profile for the new capital plan.
